In multivariate analyses, the adjusted rates of medically treated thyroid disease were increased in 2002–03 [adjusted incidence ratio (IR) 1.26, 95% CI 1.03–1.53] and 2004–05 (adjusted IR 1.22, 95% CI 0.99–1.49) compared to 1995–97. The rate of medically treated thyroid disease was lower in blacks (0.16/1000 child years) compared to whites (0.24/1000 child years) and this decreased rate was also seen in the multivariable model (adjusted IR 0.68, 95% CI 0.59–0.79). DISCUSSION Although racial disparities in the life expectancy of individuals with DS exist, overall the median life expectancy has increased dramatically in recent decades. ; Despite improvements in quality of life, people with DS remain a vulnerable population. Screening for thyroid disease has been recommended for a number of reasons including: the high prevalence in the population, the adverse medical effects associated with the disorder, and the availability of safe testing and an effective treatment. Over the 11 year study pear, the population-based incidence of medically treated thyroid disease in this cohort of over 1000 children with Down syndrome was 10.8%. Although several studies have investigated the prevalence and incidence of thyroid dysfunction in children and adults with Down syndrome, to our knowledge, this is the first population-based estimate of the incidence of medically treated thyroid disease in children with DS. ; – ; – The primary objective of this investigation was to determine whether an increase in medically treated thyroid disease occurred following re-release in February 2001 of AAP guidelines recommending annual screening for thyroid disease starting at age one year. Compared to 1995–1997, rates of medically treated thyroid disease increased 73% in 2002–2003 and 72% in 2004–2005. We determined rates of medically treated thyroid disease in a comparison cohort of children without DS, in whom an increase in identification of new cases of medically treated thyroid disease would not be expected following re-release of DS specific guidelines. In a Scottish cohort which included over 100,000 children aged 1 to 22 years, the prevalence of receiving 2 or more prescriptions for thyroid medication was 0.135% over the 3 year study period. In the TennCare cohort of children without DS, the incidence of medically treated thyroid disease over the 11 year study period was 0.21%. In contrast to the 73% increase in the cohort of children with Down syndrome there was only a 26% increase in the rate of medically treated thyroid disease in 2002–03 compared to 1995–1997. There were also differences in medically treated thyroid disease by race and age. African-American children with Down syndrome were less likely to have medically treated thyroid disease than white children. It is important to note that the decreased rate in African-Americans compared to whites was also seen in the parallel cohort of children without Down syndrome. Therefore we do not know whether racial differences in rates of medically treated thyroid disease in children with Down syndrome are due to differences in disease incidence or in screening. Lastly, there were differences in risk of medically treated thyroid disease by age group. In children with Down syndrome, all of the older age groups were less likely to have medically treated thyroid disease than the 1 to < 3 year age group. This could be the result of a number of factors, including the highest incidence occurring in this age group or the higher likelihood of undergoing screening due to multiple contacts with the healthcare system. In addition, physicians may be more likely to prescribe medication for young children with abnormal thyroid function studies as children less than age three are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of untreated hypothyroidism on intellectual development. There are several limitations to consider. The outcome of medically treated thyroid disease is dependent on screening for thyroid disease, which is likely subject to variation in physician practice. We were not able to capture screening for thyroid disease or the results of laboratory tests in this study. In addition, practice patterns may vary among physicians in treatment of abnormal thyroid function. For example, the treatment of compensated thyroid disease, a condition that may be transient, is a topic of debate. ; However this study was designed to determine the rate of medically treated thyroid disease in this population, not the appropriateness of treatment. Although we assessed the level of medically treated thyroid disease after the re-release of the policy guideline statement, we were

to variation in physician practice. We were not able to capture screening for thyroid disease or the results of laboratory tests in this study. In addition, practice patterns may vary among physicians in treatment of abnormal thyroid function. For example, the treatment of compensated thyroid disease, a condition that may be transient, is a topic of debate. ; However this study was designed to determine the rate of medically treated thyroid disease in this population, not the appropriateness of treatment. Although we assessed the level of medically treated thyroid disease after the re-release of the policy guideline statement, we were not able to directly evaluate the impact of a particular guideline on screening for thyroid disease. However, this study does provide a population based estimation of the incidence of medically treated thyroid disease and investigates the temporal relationship of the change in incidence and the re-release of guidelines. It is important to note that across the eleven year study period there were no major changes in the structure of TennCare or in how the primary outcome, prescription filled for thyroid medication, was captured. Furthermore, changes in the sensitivity of thyroid function testing were not temporally related to re-release of the guidelines. The findings may also have limited generalizability. The TennCare population in Tennessee represents individuals with disabilities, who are low-income, or unable to otherwise obtain medical insurance. Therefore, we did not capture participants with only private insurance, the uninsured, or individuals who did not seek medical care. The practice patterns of physicians that serve patients in TennCare may not reflect those of providers that primarily work with other patient populations. Therefore, the rate of medically treated thyroid disease in the TennCare cohort may not reflect the rate of children who were privately insured or that did not have any type of insurance. However, because TennCare provides insurance for children with disabilities, the study likely includes the majority of children with Down syndrome in the state. CONCLUSION A 73% increase in the rate of medically treated thyroid disease in children with Down syndrome enrolled in TennCare was seen following re-release of AAP guidelines. The population-based incidence of medically treated thyroid disease in the cohort was 10.8%, over the 11 year period 1995 to 2005. The temporal relationship suggests that the re-release of the AAP guidelines may have increased physician awareness, resulting in increased rates of screening for and identification of thyroid dysfunction.

documents.title: ATA position statement on drug-induced thyroid dysfunction

chunks.content: Introduction Acromegaly is a rare endocrine disorder caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone (GH), usually from an adenoma in the anterior pituitary gland. This condition results in elevated levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), leading to abnormal tissue growth [ , ]. Acromegaly is a slow-progressing condition that often goes undiagnosed for several years due to its subtle and non-specific early symptoms. Clinically, patients present with distinct physical changes, such as the coarsening of facial features and enlargement of the hands and feet. Beyond its characteristic physical manifestations, acromegaly affects multiple organ systems, contributing to cardiovascular, metabolic, neurologic, and respiratory complications [ ]. Common comorbidities include hypertension, insulin resistance, obstructive sleep apnea, and an increased risk of malignancies, such as colorectal cancer [ ]. In addition to systemic complications, the pituitary tumor itself can cause mechanical compression of surrounding structures, leading to symptoms such as headaches, vision disturbances (particularly bitemporal hemianopsia), cranial nerve dysfunction, and hormone deficiencies due to pituitary compression. While surgical intervention and somatostatin receptor ligands can contribute to tumor size reduction, pegvisomant regulates IGF-1 levels by blocking GH activity in peripheral tissues rather than acting on the tumor itself. Consequently, pegvisomant does not alleviate symptoms caused by the tumor’s mass effect, necessitating close monitoring in patients with significant tumor-related complications [ , ]. Surgery, primarily via a transsphenoidal approach, is the cornerstone treatment for acromegaly, aiming to remove growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas. It relieves mass effects, alleviates symptoms, and enhances the response to subsequent treatments [ , ], though normalization of IGF-1 levels is often delayed and may take months [ , ]. A meta-analysis conducted across European Reference Network centers (Endo-ERN) reviewed 48 studies from 18 pituitary centers across seven countries (2010–2019). The analysis reported a remission rate of 50% (95% CI: 42–59%) for acromegaly patients, underscoring the need for experienced surgeons and multidisciplinary management to optimize outcomes [ ]. When surgery is not feasible or incomplete, medical treatments like somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs: octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide) [ – ], dopamine receptor agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) [ ], and GH receptor antagonists (pegvisomant) are used to control GH secretion or action and normalize IGF-1 levels. In recurrent or aggressive cases where medical therapy is insufficient, radiotherapy, including conventional and stereotactic radiosurgery, may be employed [ , ]. Effective management is critical for reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with acromegaly, as patients face significant risks from musculoskeletal deformities, metabolic dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease [ , ]. Among the medical treatments available, pegvisomant, a GH receptor antagonist, plays an important role in normalizing IGF-1 levels and mitigating the biochemical effects of GH excess. It provides a useful alternative, particularly in cases where other treatments are insufficient or, more rarely, poorly suitable, such as certain genetic forms of GH excess [ – ]. This review aims to explore the role of pegvisomant in managing acromegaly, focusing on its impact on comorbidities and its benefits for improving patients' quality of life, as well as its place in clinical practice. This review was conducted through a systematic electronic literature search using the PubMed database, covering publications up to March 2025. The search strategy involved a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords, including “acromegaly,” “growth hormone,” “pituitary adenoma,” “comorbidities,” “quality of life,” “diagnosis,” “treatment,” and “pegvisomant.” Studies were selected based on relevance to the use of pegvisomant in patients with acromegaly, particularly its effects on associated comorbidities (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypertension, sleep apnea), quality of life metrics, treatment efficacy beyond insulin-like growth factor 1 normalization, and reported safety outcomes. Only peer-reviewed original articles published in English were included. After screening titles and abstracts, full texts of potentially eligible studies were reviewed. A total of 45 studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized to provide a narrative analysis. The goal was to highlight the importance of individualized management strategies to optimize patient outcomes. Pegvisomant Mechanism of action In acromegaly, chronic overproduction of GH leads to elevated levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), both of which contribute to unregulated tissue growth and a wide range of systemic complications. These include progressive somatic disfigurement and significant comorbidities that increase morbidity and mortality. [ ] [ ]. The development of pegvisomant originated from the discovery that modifying a specific glycine residue (G120) in the third alpha-helix of human growth hormone (GH) created a molecule without growth-promoting activity, effectively transforming it into a GH antagonist. Normally, GH binds to two receptor sites on the GH receptor dimer, initiating signal transduction. The G120 mutation disrupts the second binding site, preventing the formation of a trimeric complex, thereby blocking the signaling pathway. Additionally, pegvisomant has eight further modifications at the first receptor binding site, which increase its affinity for the GH receptor and give it a competitive edge over natural GH.

development of pegvisomant originated from the discovery that modifying a specific glycine residue (G120) in the third alpha-helix of human growth hormone (GH) created a molecule without growth-promoting activity, effectively transforming it into a GH antagonist. Normally, GH binds to two receptor sites on the GH receptor dimer, initiating signal transduction. The G120 mutation disrupts the second binding site, preventing the formation of a trimeric complex, thereby blocking the signaling pathway. Additionally, pegvisomant has eight further modifications at the first receptor binding site, which increase its affinity for the GH receptor and give it a competitive edge over natural GH. To prolong the drug’s half-life and reduce its clearance rate, polyethylene glycol (PEG) groups are added to the molecule, allowing pegvisomant to remain active in the body for a longer period and making it more effective in controlling the disease [ – ]. Pegvisomant exerts its effects by blocking the action of GH at the receptor level, which in turn reduces the production of IGF-I. This decrease in IGF-I levels helps to relieve the clinical symptoms associated with GH excess in acromegaly. IGF-I is the primary biomarker used to measure the effectiveness of pegvisomant as it indirectly reflects GH action [ , ]. Pegvisomant received approval in Europe in 2002 and in the United States in 2003 for treating acromegaly in patients whose condition could not be sufficiently managed through surgery, radiation therapy, or other medications. It was later authorized in the U.S. as a primary medical treatment for cases where surgery or radiation therapy either failed to control the disease or were deemed unsuitable. Biological outcomes in clinical trials The efficacy and safety of pegvisomant in treating acromegaly have been evaluated in several clinical trials, including two pivotal phase 3 studies [ – ] (Table ). In an initial phase 1, placebo-controlled trial, pegvisomant (B2036-PEG) was administered in single rising doses to 36 healthy male participants. This study demonstrated that the drug was well tolerated, with no serious or severe adverse reactions reported. At the highest dose of 1.0 mg/kg, pegvisomant reduced insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) levels by 49 ± 6% by day 5 compared to placebo (P < 0.001), while growth hormone (GH) levels remained stable if measured by a specific immunoassay which does not cross-react with pegvisomant, suggesting that pegvisomant selectively blocks peripheral GH action without disrupting GH feedback mechanisms [ ]. In a pivotal phase 3 randomized, double-blind study involving 112 patients with acromegaly, daily subcutaneous doses of pegvisomant (10 mg, 15 mg, and 20 mg) were compared with placebo over 12 weeks. IGF-I levels decreased significantly across all treatment groups, with reductions of 26.7% ± 27.9% at 10 mg, 50.1% ± 26.7% at 15 mg, and 62.5% ± 21.3% at 20 mg, compared to 4.0% ± 16.8% in the placebo group (P < 0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). IGF-I concentrations were normalized in 10% of patients in the placebo group and in 54%, 81%, and 89% of patients receiving increasing pegvisomant doses of 10 mg, 15 mg, and 20 mg, respectively. In addition to biochemical improvements, patients treated with 15 mg or 20 mg of pegvisomant showed reductions in symptoms, including soft tissue swelling, excessive perspiration, fatigue, and ring size. The incidence of adverse events was comparable between treatment and placebo groups, indicating a favorable safety profile [ ]. In a follow-up pivotal phase 3 study, 160 patients received pegvisomant for a mean of 425 days, with efficacy assessed in 152 of these individuals. After 6, 12, and 18 months of treatment, mean IGF-I levels decreased by at least 50%, and 97% of patients treated for 12 months or longer achieved normal IGF-I concentrations. Serum insulin and glucose levels also decreased significantly (P < 0.05). Growth hormone levels increased during treatment but returned to baseline within 30 days of pegvisomant withdrawal. Antibodies to GH were detected in 16.9% of patients, but no tachyphylaxis occurred. Two patients experienced tumor growth, and two others showed increased liver enzyme levels, necessitating discontinuation. Overall, pegvisomant demonstrated sustained efficacy and a generally safe profile, with no effect on tumor volume observed over time (P = 0.353) [ ]. Table displays a comprehensive summary of pivotal clinical trials evaluating the effects of pegvisomant therapy in patients with acromegaly, including study design, number of patients, endpoints, and key outcomes. Biological outcomes from real-world evidence Real-world data on pegvisomant have demonstrated consistent efficacy and safety in treating acromegaly, as reported across several observational studies from different regions ( Table ). Observational studies on pegvisomant reported IGF-I normalization in most patients (74.1% in Brazil, 62.9% in Argentina, 68.2% in Japan, and broad disease control in Germany). Glycemic improvements were notable (56.6% in Brazil), while tumor growth remained low (5.2%–9.8%) and liver enzyme elevations (9.2%–16%) were generally transient and non-severe [ ] [

Biological outcomes from real-world evidence Real-world data on pegvisomant have demonstrated consistent efficacy and safety in treating acromegaly, as reported across several observational studies from different regions ( Table ). Observational studies on pegvisomant reported IGF-I normalization in most patients (74.1% in Brazil, 62.9% in Argentina, 68.2% in Japan, and broad disease control in Germany). Glycemic improvements were notable (56.6% in Brazil), while tumor growth remained low (5.2%–9.8%) and liver enzyme elevations (9.2%–16%) were generally transient and non-severe [ ] [ – ]. The ACROSTUDY, a global non-interventional study that included 2,221 patients, provided further evidence of pegvisomant's long-term safety and efficacy. The IGF-I normalization rate increased from 11.4% at treatment initiation to 75.4% after 10 years, with tumor growth observed in 7.1% of patients and liver function abnormalities in 3.2% [ ]. Lastly, a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, published in 2019, reported that pegvisomant controlled acromegaly in 60.9% of patients overall, with better outcomes observed in those receiving monotherapy (71.7% control rate). Tumor growth and transaminase elevations were estimated at 7.3% and 3.0%, respectively. The meta-analysis concluded that real-world effectiveness is slightly lower than reported in clinical trials, but pegvisomant remains a valuable treatment option for acromegaly, particularly as monotherapy [ ]. The role of pegvisomant in managing acromegaly-related comorbidities Cardiovascular comorbidities Cardiomyopathy is a classical comorbidity of acromegaly [ ]. Pegvisomant has shown promising effects on cardiovascular health, particularly by improving cardiac function. A study examined long-term therapy with pegvisomant and found significant cardiac improvements. Among patients with low baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≤ 60%), LVEF significantly improved, while those with LVEF > 70% experienced a decrease, suggesting normalization. Left ventricular mass index (LVMi) decreased significantly from 123 ± 25 to 101 ± 21 g/m 2 (P < 0.05) in 17 patients with elevated baseline LVMi (> 91 g/m 2 ), while remaining stable in others. Additionally, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels normalized in 29 of 42 patients (69%) at the first cardiac evaluation, conducted 20 ± 16 months after starting therapy [ ] (Table ) (Tables , , , and ). A study highlighted the vascular benefits of pegvisomant in acromegalic patients resistant to somatostatin analogues. After 18 months of treatment, carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) decreased slightly from 1.18 ± 0.59 mm to 0.97 ± 0.17 mm, though this change was not statistically significant. Brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD) significantly improved from 7.5 ± 2.5% to 8.8 ± 3.7% (P = 0.016). Baseline values of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, serum glucose, insulin, and HOMA index, which were elevated compared to controls, showed significant reductions post-treatment, while lipid profiles remained unchanged [ ] (Table ). Some cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, are also alleviated by pegvisomant therapy. In a German study assessing cardiovascular risk factors in acromegaly, patients exhibited higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP) compared to matched controls (P < 0.001). Following 12 months of pegvisomant therapy, systolic BP showed a significant reduction (P = 0.04), contributing to an overall decrease in the Framingham risk score (FRS) (P = 0.005), a widely used tool that estimates the 10-year risk of developing coronary heart disease based on factors such as age, BP, cholesterol levels, and diabetes status. IGF-I normalization was achieved in 62% of patients (41 of 62), and in these individuals, both systolic and diastolic BP were significantly lower compared to those with partially controlled IGF-I, highlighting the relationship between effective disease control and reduced cardiovascular risk [ ] (Table ). This improvement is critical, as a high Framingham risk score (FRS) has been linked to increased coronary artery calcification (CAC) in acromegaly patients, and pegvisomant could help mitigate this risk [ ] (Table ). Long-term pegvisomant treatment has been shown to improve acromegalic cardiomyopathy by reducing left ventricular hypertrophy and enhancing both diastolic and systolic function. In a study of 17 patients, LVMi significantly decreased, with the prevalence of left ventricular hypertrophy dropping from 50 to 17% after 18 months. Cardiac insufficiency, initially present in 76% of patients, was reduced to 8%. Additionally, improved IGF-I control correlated with enhanced ejection fraction and overall cardiac performance, highlighting the cardiovascular benefits of GH receptor antagonism in acromegaly [ ] (Table ). In a study evaluating the effects of pegvisomant on arrhythmias in acromegaly, long-term treatment significantly reduced heart rate parameters (heart rate (HR), mean heart rate (MHR), and minimal heart rate (mHR)) after 18 months. A correlation was observed between heart rate reduction and decreased left ventricular mass. Additionally, arrhythmias resolved in one patient and improved in another, while the prevalence of conduction disturbances dropped from 15% to 7.7%, highlighting the potential benefits of GH receptor antagonism on cardiac electrophysiology

enhanced ejection fraction and overall cardiac performance, highlighting the cardiovascular benefits of GH receptor antagonism in acromegaly [ ] (Table ). In a study evaluating the effects of pegvisomant on arrhythmias in acromegaly, long-term treatment significantly reduced heart rate parameters (heart rate (HR), mean heart rate (MHR), and minimal heart rate (mHR)) after 18 months. A correlation was observed between heart rate reduction and decreased left ventricular mass. Additionally, arrhythmias resolved in one patient and improved in another, while the prevalence of conduction disturbances dropped from 15% to 7.7%, highlighting the potential benefits of GH receptor antagonism on cardiac electrophysiology [ ] (Table ). In a study investigating cardiovascular risk markers in acromegaly, 48 patients and 47 matched controls were assessed. At baseline, patients with acromegaly had significantly lower median CRP levels compared to controls [0.3 (0.2–0.8) vs. 2.0 (0.6–3.7) mg/L; P < 0.0001] and higher insulin levels [78.6 (55.8–130.2) vs. 54.5 (36.6–77.5) pM; P = 0.0051]. During the placebo-controlled phase, patients treated with 20 mg/day pegvisomant showed a significant increase in CRP compared to placebo (13.7 ± 3.6 vs. 0.5 ± 3.3 mg/L; P = 0.010). In the 18-month open-label extension (median 15.6 months), CRP increased by 2.0 ± 0.5 mg/L (P = 0.0002), total cholesterol by 0.22 ± 0.11 mM (P = 0.050), and triglycerides by 0.25 ± 0.09 mM (P = 0.007), while lipoprotein(a) decreased by 70 ± 33 mg/L (P = 0.039). No significant changes were observed in IL-6, homocysteine, glucose, insulin, HDL, or LDL cholesterol levels [ ]. Metabolic comorbidities Metabolic dysfunction, especially insulin resistance and diabetes, is frequently encountered in acromegaly patients. Pegvisomant’s positive impact on glucose metabolism and effects on lipid profile is well-documented. In the German study involving 133 acromegalic patients compared to 665 controls, pegvisomant treatment was associated with significant metabolic improvements. At baseline, patients exhibited elevated glycosylated hemoglobin levels and a higher prevalence of diabetes mellitus compared to controls (P < 0.001). After 12 months of treatment, glycosylated hemoglobin levels decreased significantly (P = 0.02). Insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) normalization was achieved in 62% of patients (41 of 62), and in these individuals, glucose levels were significantly lower compared to those with partially controlled IGF-I [ ]. A study in type 2 diabetic acromegalic patients showed that pegvisomant normalized IGF-I levels slightly less often in diabetic patients compared to non-diabetic patients, with higher doses required for normalization. In this study, pegvisomant also significantly decreased HbA1c levels during the first 6 months of treatment. These findings suggest that diabetic patients achieve normalization less frequently than non-diabetic patients and require higher doses of pegvisomant to reach similar outcomes [ ]. Another study focusing on type 1 diabetic patients found that pegvisomant improved hepatic insulin sensitivity and reduced intramyocellular lipid content in muscle, further underscoring its metabolic benefits [ ]. Similar results were obtained in a small study where pegvisomant reduced overnight free fatty acid concentrations and improved insulin sensitivity, indicating its efficacy in countering the insulin-desensitizing effects of GH excess [ ]. Notably, pegvisomant and SRLs differ in their impact on glucose metabolism in acromegaly. Pegvisomant improves insulin sensitivity by directly blocking GH action, without suppressing insulin secretion, preserving pancreatic β-cell function. In contrast, SRLs may suppress insulin secretion by activating somatostatin receptors on β-cells, often leading to hyperglycemia despite their ability to lower GH levels. This distinction highlights pegvisomant’s unique advantage in managing glucose metabolism in acromegaly, as it not only enhances insulin sensitivity but also avoids the deleterious effects on insulin secretion observed with SRLs [ ]. An analysis from the ACROSTUDY evaluated the effects of pegvisomant on glucose metabolism in 1,762 acromegaly patients, including 510 with pre-existing diabetes mellitus (DM). After one year, the mean blood glucose in the DM group decreased from 140.0 to 116.4 mg/dL, and HbA1c levels showed a modest reduction (7.0% to 6.8% at four years). IGF-I normalization was achieved in 52.1% and 57.4% of patients with and without DM, respectively. Pegvisomant was well tolerated across both groups, with patients with DM requiring slightly higher doses (18.2 vs. 15.3 mg/day). These findings suggest that pegvisomant contributes to moderate improvements in glucose metabolism while effectively controlling IGF-I levels in acromegaly [ ]. Finally, in a cohort of 20 patients with active acromegaly (mean age 58.7 years), pegvisomant treatment significantly reduced mean serum IGF-I from 585.2 ± 54.3 to 169.2 ± 13.9 ng/mL (P < 0.0001). Following IGF-I normalization, total cholesterol increased from 5.0 ± 0.3 to 5.7 ± 0.4 mmol/L (P = 0.0068), LDL cholesterol from 3.0 ± 0.25 to 3.7 ± 0.31 mmol/L (P = 0.0093), and apolipoprotein B from 110.6 ± 7.76 to 127.1 ± 8.86 mg/L (P = 0.014). Apolipoprotein A1 rose from 153 ± 4 to 166.4 ± 5.43 mg/L (P = 0.026), while median Lp(a) decreased from 342 to 235

Following IGF-I normalization, total cholesterol increased from 5.0 ± 0.3 to 5.7 ± 0.4 mmol/L (P = 0.0068), LDL cholesterol from 3.0 ± 0.25 to 3.7 ± 0.31 mmol/L (P = 0.0093), and apolipoprotein B from 110.6 ± 7.76 to 127.1 ± 8.86 mg/L (P = 0.014). Apolipoprotein A1 rose from 153 ± 4 to 166.4 ± 5.43 mg/L (P = 0.026), while median Lp(a) decreased from 342 to 235 mg/L (P = 0.0035). Despite these changes, HDL and triglyceride levels remained stable. Fasting insulin levels dropped from 9.9 to 8.3 mU/L (P < 0.001), and insulin resistance improved significantly (HOMA-IR from 2.7 to 1.9; P < 0.001). These findings suggest that while pegvisomant normalizes lipid profiles altered by active acromegaly, its long-term cardiovascular implications require further study [ ]. Musculoskeletal and skeletal health The heightened risk of vertebral fractures (VFs) in acromegaly patients is a significant concern. Pegvisomant has demonstrated some ability to reduce this risk. In a longitudinal study, pegvisomant therapy was associated with a reduction in the incidence of VFs, dropping from 43.9% to 26.8% in patients previously treated with somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs). However, the presence of pre-existing fractures remained a strong predictor for future fractures [ ]. In a cross-sectional study of 38 acromegalic patients on pegvisomant therapy, 31.6% had vertebral fractures. Fractures were associated with longer disease duration (P = 0.01), higher pegvisomant doses (P = 0.008), and untreated hypogonadism (P = 0.02). In males, fractures correlated with pegvisomant dose (P = 0.02) and hypogonadism (P = 0.02), while in females, they were linked to active disease (P = 0.03), elevated IGF-I (P = 0.01), and the d3GHR polymorphism (P = 0.005). IGF-I levels and disease control were similar between males (1.7 ± 3 standard deviation scores [SDS]) and females (2.6 ± 4.2 SDS; P = 0.54), with controlled disease rates of 76% and 80%, respectively (P = 0.71). In females, IGF-I/SDS was significantly associated with vertebral fractures (odds ratio: 1.86; CI 95% 1.05–3.3; P = 0.02). Bone mineral density was not significantly related to fractures, suggesting fractures are more influenced by disease activity and hypogonadism than by bone density [ ]. Interestingly, pegvisomant was shown not to affect osteoblast function or bone development in vitro, indicating that its beneficial effects on bone health may be secondary to IGF-I normalization rather than direct action on bone cells [ ]. A study evaluating the effects of long-term pegvisomant on bone health in acromegaly found mixed effects on bone mineral density (BMD) and microstructure. Over a median of approximately 7 years, lumbar spine BMD improved, while hip BMD decreased in men. After ~ 9 years, patients exhibited larger bones but lower trabecular and cortical volumetric density with disrupted microarchitecture compared to healthy controls e.g., at the radius: ∼47% greater cortical area [P = 0.0002], ∼20% lower trabecular volumetric BMD [P = 0.007], and trabecular bone volume fraction [P = 0.01]; trabecular number and thickness were 18% [P = 0.001] and 15% [P = 0.003] lower, respectively; cortical thickness and trabecular separation were 62% [P < 0.0001] and 40% [P = 0.002] higher, respectively. At the tibia: trabecular volumetric BMD was 17% [P = 0.015] and bone volume fraction 14% [P = 0.04] lower; cortical thickness, trabecular thickness, and separation were 12% [P = 0.003], 8.4% [P = 0.007], and 35% [P = 0.008] higher; trabecular number was 16.6% lower [P = 0.01]). However, bone microstructure was similar to that of non-pegvisomant-treated acromegaly patients, and bone turnover markers (BTMs) stabilized over time. These findings suggest that while pegvisomant does not worsen bone microstructure, deficits in bone quality persist, potentially contributing to fracture risk in acromegaly [ ]. Respiratory comorbidities Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a frequent complication of acromegaly, often caused by soft tissue overgrowth and craniofacial changes. A study of 12 patients with active acromegaly evaluated the effects of pegvisomant over 6 months on sleep apnea and tongue volume. IGF1 levels significantly decreased from 407 ± 114 to 199 ± 23 µg/L (P = 0.0001). Tongue volume was reduced from 105 ± 33 to 83 ± 33 ml (P = 0.007), accompanied by a decrease in the apnoea-hypopnoea index from 23 ± 22 to 18 ± 18 episodes/hour (P = 0.0066). Mandibular length was correlated with the initial tongue volume (r 2 = 0.6072, P = 0.0028). These findings suggest that pegvisomant reduces tongue volume, improving sleep-disordered breathing in poorly controlled acromegaly [ ]. In another study, pegvisomant reduced the apnea–hypopnea index and even resolved OSA in a subset of patients, further highlighting its role in improving respiratory function in acromegaly [ ]. IGF-I—insulin-like growth factor I;; OSA—obstructive sleep apnea. Neurological comorbidities Although the direct impact of pegvisomant on neurological issues such as carpal tunnel syndrome has not been extensively studied, improvements in soft tissue swelling after one year of treatment have been noted in one report from the German Pegvisomant Observational Study, indicating that pegvisomant may have a role in addressing neurological complications related to tissue overgrowth [ ]. However, in the ACROSTUDY extension, a real-world observational study, the patients experienced minor improvements in symptoms such as soft tissue swelling. Impact of pegvisomant on the quality of life of patients with acromegaly Acromegaly significantly impairs patients' quality of life (QoL), affecting both physical and psychological aspects due to symptoms like fatigue, joint pain, and soft tissue swelling. Several studies have investigated the impact of pegvisomant on QoL: A Spanish study found that QoL improvement was the primary factor influencing treatment choices in 37% of patients, with 95% preferring pegvisomant as a second-line treatment due to its efficacy in IGF-I control and symptom reduction [ ]. Another study reported significant QoL enhancements in patients with persistent symptoms despite normalized IGF-I levels, indicating pegvisomant's role in alleviating residual symptoms [ ]. A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study demonstrated that adding weekly pegvisomant to somatostatin analog (SSA) therapy improved physical and overall QoL scores, reducing perspiration and soft tissue swelling, even without significant changes in IGF-I levels [ ]. Conversely, a cross-sectional study revealed that pegvisomant users reported lower satisfaction with treatment convenience, likely due to daily injections; however, overall treatment satisfaction was positively correlated with QoL scores [ ]. The ACROSTUDY extension, a real-world observational study, showed minor improvements in symptoms like soft tissue swelling, perspiration, and fatigue, with no significant difference in QoL scores based on IGF-I control, suggesting benefits may be somewhat independent of strict biochemical normalization [ ]. A study of 116 acromegaly patients switching to pegvisomant due to SSA failure found comparable QoL scores between pegvisomant and SSA-treated patients, with higher HbA1c, BMI, and IGF-I Z-scores correlating with poorer QoL (BMI 30 ± 6 kg/m2, and male sex 38%). Mean IGF-1 Z-scores were higher in ACTIVE (3.9 ± 1.0) vs SSA and PEG, which did not differ from one another (0.5 ± 0.7 and 0.5 ± 0.7, P < 0.0001 vs ACTIVE)) [ ]. Another study examining psychological QoL aspects found that patients achieving biochemical control, whether via surgery or medical therapy, reported improved psychological well-being. Pegvisomant was particularly effective in enhancing self-perception of physical appearance, reinforcing its role in overall QoL improvement [ ]. It's important to note that treatment satisfaction is subjective and can be influenced by factors such as treatment burden and individual patient expectations. Discontinuation rates are notable; approximately 25% of patients discontinue treatment or are lost to follow-up, with up to 88% of these cases having uncontrolled disease, reflecting potential treatment weariness and the need for therapies that balance efficacy with patient convenience [ ]. Discussion The cumulative evidence from this review underscores the significant role pegvisomant plays in the management of acromegaly, particularly as a monotherapy for patients who fail or cannot tolerate first-line treatments like somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs). Pegvisomant’s unique mechanism of action as a growth hormone (GH) receptor antagonist allows it to directly inhibit peripheral GH signaling, leading to normalization of insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) levels and subsequent improvements across multiple health domains [ – ]. Pegvisomant and SRLs are both utilized in acromegaly management, each with distinct mechanisms and efficacy profiles. SRLs, including first-generation agents like octreotide and lanreotide, primarily inhibit growth hormone secretion by targeting somatostatin receptors, achieving IGF-I normalization in approximately 55% of patients. Second-generation SRLs, such as pasireotide, offer broader receptor affinity but are associated with higher rates of hyperglycemia. In contrast, pegvisomant directly blocks GH receptors, leading to IGF-I normalization in up to 97% of cases, making it particularly effective for patients unresponsive to SRLs. However, pegvisomant requires daily subcutaneous injections and monitoring for potential liver enzyme elevations. While SRLs may reduce tumor size due to their antiproliferative effects, pegvisomant does not typically influence tumor volume. Therefore, treatment selection should be individualized, considering factors like efficacy, side effect profiles, administration routes, and patient preferences [ ]. In terms of

In contrast, pegvisomant directly blocks GH receptors, leading to IGF-I normalization in up to 97% of cases, making it particularly effective for patients unresponsive to SRLs. However, pegvisomant requires daily subcutaneous injections and monitoring for potential liver enzyme elevations. While SRLs may reduce tumor size due to their antiproliferative effects, pegvisomant does not typically influence tumor volume. Therefore, treatment selection should be individualized, considering factors like efficacy, side effect profiles, administration routes, and patient preferences [ ]. In terms of comorbidities, pegvisomant has demonstrated broad efficacy. Cardiovascular outcomes have shown significant improvements, including reduced left ventricular mass and enhanced ejection fraction in patients with compromised cardiac function [ ]. Studies have also reported a reduction in carotid intima-media thickness and improved brachial artery flow-mediated dilation, suggesting pegvisomant's vascular benefits [ ]. Moreover, its ability to normalize blood pressure and improve glycemic control, particularly in diabetic patients, highlights its role in addressing both metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors [ ]. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings in larger cohorts and over longer treatment durations. Pegvisomant has also shown promise in musculoskeletal health, reducing the risk of vertebral fractures in some patients transitioning from SRLs. While this effect is encouraging, fracture risk appears to be more strongly influenced by disease activity and untreated hypogonadism than by bone density, emphasizing the need for comprehensive management of these factors [ – ]. Respiratory benefits have also been noted, with pegvisomant reducing tongue volume and improving obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, further enhancing its utility in managing acromegaly-related complications [ ]. In addition to its impact on physical health, pegvisomant has been shown to improve the quality of life (QoL) for acromegalic patients. Studies highlight significant reductions in symptoms such as soft tissue swelling, excessive perspiration, and fatigue, which persist despite normalized IGF-I levels with other treatments. Interestingly, improvements in QoL have been observed even in the absence of full biochemical control, suggesting that pegvisomant may exert benefits beyond IGF-I normalization [ – ]. This underscores the importance of addressing patient-perceived health and residual symptoms as part of a holistic treatment strategy. Despite these benefits, pegvisomant therapy is not without limitations. The daily injectable nature of the treatment can be inconvenient for some patients, impacting adherence and overall satisfaction. However, pegvisomant has a long elimination half-life (~ 74–172 h), which allows less-frequent dosing in selected patients [ ]. Prospective data show that patients biochemically controlled on daily pegvisomant can maintain normal IGF-I after switching to higher-dose regimens given twice weekly and then once weekly, without loss of efficacy or tolerability [ ]. Weekly pegvisomant is also effective when combined with long-acting somatostatin receptor ligands, typically titrated around 80 mg/week (range ~ 40–120 mg/week), with durable biochemical control and acceptable safety in long-term follow-up [ , ]. Such extended schedules may reduce injection burden and support adherence. Its high cost also remains a significant barrier, raising questions about cost-effectiveness in certain healthcare settings. In a randomized trial comparing combination and monotherapy regimens, the mean monthly cost was lowest with low-dose SRL plus once-weekly pegvisomant (USD 9,837 ± 1,375), higher with high-dose SRL plus weekly pegvisomant (USD 14,261 ± 1,645), and highest with daily pegvisomant (USD 22,543 ± 11,158), while IGF-I control was maintained in 96% of evaluable patients [ ]. In a French cost-utility model, pegvisomant had an incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR) of €27,805/QALY versus pasireotide, whereas pegvisomant + first-generation SRL had an ICUR of €253,854/QALY versus pegvisomant alone [ ]. These data suggest that although pegvisomant is clinically effective, the economic impact varies by regimen and health-system context and may affect adherence, particularly in settings with greater out-of-pocket costs. Additionally, while real-world evidence supports its safety profile, concerns regarding tumor growth and liver enzyme elevations require ongoing monitoring.An under-discussed side effect of pegvisomant is lipodystrophy at injection sites, which can limit the drug's action and lead to treatment discontinuation. Cases have been reported where lipohypertrophy developed during therapy, but these were reversible upon discontinuation or with proper injection site rotation techniques [ – ]. Adherence to pegvisomant therapy remains a critical factor in achieving optimal disease control. A multicenter observational study in Spain found that adherence rates varied widely (60.7–92.1%) and were not directly correlated with biochemical control. Notably, older age and alternative dosing schedules (other than daily administration) were associated with lower adherence. Despite overall high treatment satisfaction (SATMED-Q score: 74.6 ± 15.4/100) and convenience ratings (71.2 ± 15.2/100), 34.3% of patients made errors in the reconstitution or administration process, potentially impacting therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the importance of not only monitoring adherence but also ensuring proper medication administration, as errors in injection technique may compromise treatment outcomes [ ]. Notably, older age and alternative dosing schedules (other than daily administration) were associated with lower adherence. Despite overall high treatment satisfaction (SATMED-Q score: 74.6 ± 15.4/100) and convenience ratings (71.2 ± 15.2/100), 34.3% of patients made errors in the reconstitution or administration process, potentially impacting therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the importance of not only monitoring adherence but also ensuring proper medication administration, as errors in injection technique may compromise treatment outcomes [ ]. While this review focuses mainly on the role of pegvisomant as a monotherapy, its use in combination with SRLs has also been explored. Combination therapy may offer additional benefits in selected patients, particularly those with partial responses to SRLs, by providing complementary mechanisms of action. Combination therapy of somatostatin analogues with pegvisomant has been evaluated in a meta-analysis of prospective studies, showing IGF-1 normalization in 66% (95% CI 52–78%) of patients not controlled on high-dose somatostatin analogues. Glucose parameters were overall neutral (no significant change in fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c), with a decrease in fasting insulin, and elevated liver enzymes in ~ 14% of cases, underscoring the need for liver-function monitoring during therapy [ ]. However, further studies are needed to better define the indications and long-term outcomes of this approach. In the management of acromegaly, several factors can limit the efficacy of pegvisomant therapy. Obesity and diabetes mellitus are notable considerations; while pegvisomant has been shown to improve insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, the presence of these conditions may necessitate careful monitoring and dose adjustments to achieve optimal outcomes. The integration of personalized medicine into acromegaly management may enhance treatment outcomes by optimizing drug selection based on predictive biomarkers. The Spanish ACROFAST study demonstrated that a biomarker-based treatment protocol, incorporating factors such as the short acute octreotide test and tumor MRI characteristics, led to a significantly higher hormonal control rate (78% vs. 53%) and faster disease control compared to the standard trial-and-error approach. These findings highlight the potential of precision medicine in guiding therapy choices, reducing time to biochemical control, and improving overall patient outcomes [ ]. In conclusion, current data suggest that pegvisomant has a beneficial impact on certain comorbidities associated with acromegaly, such as improved metabolic profiles and potential bone health benefits. However, the evidence remains limited, and further studies are needed to fully elucidate its long-term effects on comorbidities and quality of life (QoL). Additional research should also explore its optimal use in specific patient populations and its potential role in combination therapy regimens. While biochemical control of acromegaly is essential, not all comorbidities are fully reversible, even with IGF-I normalization. Conditions such as joint disease and sleep apnea often persist despite effective treatment, including pegvisomant, due to irreversible structural changes. This highlights the need for a multidisciplinary approach to manage long-term complications beyond hormonal control, emphasizing symptom management and adjunctive therapies to improve patient outcomes [ , ] [ ].

chunks.content: Background In addition to their common manifestations, almost all inherited endocrine tumor syndromes present features of bone and mineral metabolism, either as secondary complications of primary tumors or as a primary consequence of gene mutation. There are few descriptions of these bone phenotypes in literature, and a review is still missing. This paper reviewed skeletal and mineral metabolism complications in hereditary endocrine tumor syndromes, focusing also on a description of the in vitro and in animal model studies investigating the direct role of genes, responsible for syndromes, in bone modeling and remodeling and/or in mineral metabolism homeostasis. Discussion Hereditary endocrine tumors Endocrine tumors originate from specialized hormone-secreting cells. Most of these neoplasms specialize in synthesizing and secreting hormones (functioning tumors; FTs) and only a small portion lose the hormone-secretive ability (non-functioning tumors; NFTs). Few patients without a clinical family history develop endocrine tumors (sporadic forms), while most cases have mendelian heritability (inherited forms). Inherited forms can be non-syndromic (only a single affected endocrine organ during lifetime) or syndromic (multiple tumors in endocrine and non-endocrine organs during lifetime). All syndromes have an autosomal dominant inheritance. Hereditary non-syndromic forms include familial primary hyperparathyroidism (FPHPT), familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC), familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA), and familial acromegaly (FA). Hereditary syndromic forms include Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1, type 2 A and B and type 4 (MEN1, MEN2A, MEN2B and MEN4), von Hippel Lindau (VHL), hereditary Paraganglioma/Pheochromocytoma syndromes (PGL/PCC), Hyperparathyroidism-Jaw Tumor syndrome (HPT-JT), Cowden syndrome (CS), Carney Complex (CNC), Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC), and Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 MEN1 is characterized by: 1) adenomas of parathyroid/adenomas of parathyroid (affecting over 90% of patients by the age of 50 and causing primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), which can be associated with hypercalcemia); 2) adenomas of adenohypophysis (mainly prolactin-secreting adenoma or, more rarely, non-functioning macroadenomas); 3) neuroendocrine tumors of gastro-entero-pancreatic tract (GEP-NETs) [ ]; (Table ). MEN1 is caused by germinal heterozygote inactivating mutations of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene, encoding a nuclear protein (menin) that exerts key functions in the regulation of important biological processes (cell cycle, DNA repair, apoptosis, gene transcription, and osteoblast differentiation) [ ]; (Table ). Menin interacts with many different proteins and is involved in the regulation of numerous molecular pathways, opening the possibility to have a wide spectrum of potential targets for molecular therapy of the syndrome. To date, in vivo studies on pancreatic NETs have shown efficacy towards epigenetic modulators such as bromo- and extra terminal domain (BET) inhibitors, Wnt pathway targeting β-catenin antagonists, VEGF-signalling and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) antagonists [ ]. Bone phenotype in MEN1 Osteoporosis and osteopenia are frequent, early complications in MEN1 patients (Table ]; reduction of bone mass is a common early clinical sign in MEN1 women by the age of 35 [ ]. PHPT is the main cause of bone loss. The anticipated development of PHPT (20–30 years) can significantly interfere with the achievement of normal peak of bone mass, and untreated prolonged excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases bone resorption, leading to early loss of cortical and trabecular bone. Early treatment of symptomatic PHPT, by successful subtotal parathyroid surgery, reduces skeletal damage, with significant improvement to BMD in the first 12 months [ ]. Additional conditions may be considered risk factors for osteoporosis, such as hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, hypocortisolism due to pituitary disorders, as well as malabsorption caused by surgical resection of the proximal tract of the small intestine [ ]. Despite a milder biochemical presentation, bone alterations in MEN1 PHPT are more severe than sporadic PHPT [ ], indicating that bone phenotype in MEN1 is not just a secondary consequence of PHPT and suggesting a direct role of the MEN1 gene in bone physiology regulation. Surgical removal of parathyroid adenomas, responsible for PHPT is the treatment of choice for restoring normal PTH secretion and serum level of calcium; parathyroidectomy demonstrated to normalize bone and mineral metabolism parameters. Medical therapy with cinacalcet demonstrated to be effective to control PTH over-secretion, and subsequent hypercalcemia, in patients who manifest PHPT recurrence or persistence despite one or more reoperations and in patients who are not suitable for parathyroidectomy. This calcimimetic molecule increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor to extracellular calcium and induces a decrease in PTH secretion being able to normalize parathyroid functionality and, thus, bone turn-over. Heterozygous knock-out (KO) mice for the Men1 gene ( Men1 +/− ) showed a significant reduction in BMD, trabecular bone volume and cortical bone thickness, compared to control mice [ ]. Role of the <italic toggle="yes">MEN1</italic> gene in bone phenotypes Several studies, performed in MEN1 mice models and in cells, have confirmed direct important functions of wild type menin in regulation of osteogenesis and maintenance of bone mass. Heterozygous knock-out (KO) mice for the Men1 gene ( Men1 +/− ) showed a significant reduction in BMD, trabecular bone volume and cortical bone thickness, compared to control mice [ ]. In Men1 +/− mice, the number of osteoblasts and osteoclasts and rate of mineralization were reduced, while the number of osteocytes was increased [ ]. Conversely, transgenic mice induced to over-express menin showed an increase in bone mass, number of osteoblasts, and rate of mineralization [ ]. Menin directly interacts with JunD, a transcription factor involved in negative control of cell proliferation and regulation of bone metabolism, repressing its activity [ ]. JunD-deficient mice showed increased bone mass and trabecular number, associated with increased osteoblast activity [ ]. The upregulation of JunD, caused by menin deficiency, could directly alter bone metabolism in MEN1 patients. Menin has been shown to balance the commitment of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to osteogenic or myogenic lineages. In response to BMP2, menin enhances the transcriptional activity of SMAD1/5factors, promoting osteoblastic differentiation of MSCs. Moreover, under the effect of TGF-β1, menin reinforces repression of myogenic differentiation mediated by SMAD3/TGFβ1 [ ]. When osteoblast activity is required, the expression of menin, in MSCs, is over-regulated. A reduction of wild type menin expression in these precursors can induce myogenesis [ ]. Menin acts as direct positive regulator of miR-26a [ ], a microRNA that negatively regulates the expression of SMAD1 protein during osteoblastic differentiation of MSCs [ ]. Wild type menin directly increases the transcriptional activity of two steroid receptors exerting an important role in bone modeling and remodeling [the vitamin D receptor (VDR) and estrogen receptor α (ERα)]. In parathyroid cells, vitamin D inhibits PTH transcription and cell proliferation; a reduction of VDR activity, following the loss of menin, could represent a facilitation for the growth of parathyroid cells and adenoma development [ ]. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 MEN 2 includes two clinical subtypes: 2A (MEN2A) and 2B (MEN2B) [ ]. MEN2 tumors are medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma (PHEO) and, only in MEN2A, parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, associated with PHPT [ ]; (Table ]. MEN2 is caused by germinal heterozygote activating point mutations of the proto-oncogene RET (REarranged during Transfection; 10q11.21) (Table ], encoding the homonym trans-membrane tyrosine kinase receptor (RET) responsible for positive regulation of cell growth. Different mutations are responsible for different clinical phenotypes. MEN2A patients have mutations at codons 634 (85% of cases), 609, 611, 618 and 620 [ ]. Over 90% of MEN2B patients present the de novo M918T mutation [ – ]; mutation at codon 883 (A883F) affects about 5% of MEN2B patients. Since the early 2000s, targeted medical therapies have been introduced in MEN2 patients, especially designed for the treatment of MTC. They consists of anti-angiogenic drugs and multi-targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibitors, not specifically directed against RET; for this reason the overall effectiveness is reduced and the incidence of drug resistance and side effects are increased [ ]. Recently, quinazoline compounds, specific inhibitors of the RET thyrosine kinase pathway showed mild to significant anticancer efficacy in some tumor cell lines, including thyroid cancer, suggesting a possible future therapeutic potential in MEN2 [ ]. Bone phenotype in MEN2 Skeletal affection in MEN2A is caused by PHPT, consisting in early reduction of BMD and increased risk of fracture [ , ]. PTH normalization, following surgical removal of parathyroid adenoma, reverts the bone mass loss [ ]. PHPT in MEN2A is usually milder than in MEN1 and BMD loss is less common and less severe [ ]. MEN2B phenotype is characterized by typical musculoskeletal abnormalities, including marfanoid habitus with tall and slender body, long limbs, ogival palate, and long and thin face with prognathism. Bone abnormalities, such as pectus excavatum, hollow foot, equinovarus foot, femoral epiphysiolysis, kyphosis, scoliosis and increased joint laxity, are also present [ ]; (Table ). For MEN2A-PHPT therapy with cinacalcet can be considered, with the same indication of MEN1. Not specific RET-targeted drugs for correction of bone affections in MEN2B patients are available or under evaluation, yet. In fact, up-regulation of chondromodulin-1 (CHM1), a cartilaginous and bone growth regulator protein, normally expressed in proliferating and pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes of growth plates, was observed only in MTC samples of MEN2B patients. Increased transcription of CHM1 could be a direct result of signaling alterations secondary to the RET intracellular mutation, suggesting a possible relationship, not yet determined, between the two genes [ ]. All MEN2B patients with skeletal anomalies had high expression of CHM1 [ ]; (Table ). In bone explants, the over-expression of CHM1 promotes cartilage deposition and inhibits bone formation. Chm1 mutant mice showed increased bone deposition [ ]. Altered expression of CHM1 is suspected to alter the bone growth plate, leading to the skeletal abnormalities observed in MEN2B patients. Activating mutations of the intracellular domain of RET could also be suspected to be responsible for the overexpression, in MEN2, of stanniocalcin-1 (STC1), a protein involved in the regulation of bone metabolism, by acting as an autocrine/paracrine regulator of calcium and phosphate homeostasis, with a role in early skeletal patterning and joint formation, [ ]. The high expression of STC1 during embryogenesis could be associated with the marfanoid skeletal phenotype. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 4 MEN4 is characterized by multiple parathyroid tumors with associated PHPT (81% of cases) and adenohypophysial tumors (42%; ACTHoma with Cushing syndrome, GHoma, PRLoma, and non-functioning pituitary adenoma) (Table ). Adrenal, renal and reproductive organ tumors, gastric and bronchial carcinoids and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome are also documented [ ]. MEN4 is caused by inactivating heterozygous mutations of the CDKN1B tumor suppressor gene (12p13.1) (Table ], encoding the p27 kip1 protein, a CDK2 cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, which acts as a negative regulator of cell cycle progression at G1-S checkpoint [ ]. Mutations create an altered or truncated p27 kip1 that is localized within the cytosol instead of the nucleus (contrary to the wild type counterpart), where it is not able to bind CDK2 [ ]. Currently, only 19 cases of MEN4 have been described worldwide and, thus, no sufficient data are available about the efficacy of medical therapies for this syndrome. Therapeutic approaches follow the same guidelines of MEN1, and no specific research about possible gene therapies in patients with CDKN1B mutations has been carried out yet. Application of p27 gene therapy was tested in human glioblastoma cells through CDKN1B-containing adenoviral vector transfection, showing promising anti-proliferation effects [ ]. This finding can be a starting point for future research in p27 gene therapy also for MEN4 patients. Bone phenotype in MEN4 Given the small number of MEN4 cases reported to date, no targeted studies on bone complications have been specifically conducted and data are not yet available in literature. However, since MEN4 presents a clinical phenotype overlapping that of MEN1, it is highly probable that PHPT-related hypercalcemia can alter bone metabolism and reduce BMD value the same way we find in MEN1 patients (Table ). Functional studies have shown that p27 Kip1 modulates the regulation of skeletal development and osteoblastic bone formation with a mechanism that implies its direct interaction with the PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) [ ]. The deletion of p27 kip1 in Pthrp KI mice appears to partially compensate for bone growth defect and restore osteoblastic differentiation, increasing endochondral ossification and osteogenesis (Table ), suggesting a possible future use of NLS and C-terminal regions of PTHrP to promote bone growth [ ]. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome VHL predisposes development of various malignant and benign tumors, specifically, retinal, cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas, renal carcinomas (RCC), PHEO, and pancreatic tumors (Table ). Hemangiomas of the adrenal glands, lungs and liver, and multiple cysts of the pancreas and kidneys, have been also described [ ]. VHL is caused by inactivating mutations in the tumor suppressor gene VHL (3p25.3) (Table ), encoding the homologous protein (pVHL), which can be totally absent or inactive [ ]. Normally, pVHL negatively regulates the hypoxia inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) responsible for cellular responses to hypoxia, including development of neoangiogenesis and induction of cell proliferation. Loss of wild type pVHL prevents degradation of HIF factors and induces responses to hypoxia, even when not physiologically required, inducing cell growth and formation of new vessels, thus favoring tumorigenesis [ ]. Molecular therapy in VHL is precisely targeted towards genes regulated by HIF-1α, such as VEGF, PDGF-β and TGF-α, which have a fundamental role in tumorigenesis and angiogenesis. However, if anti-VEGF drugs, as bevacizumab, or multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, as sunitinib, have shown proven efficacy towards sporadic forms of cerebellar hemangioma, pancreatic NETs and RCC, a specific role of these agents in VHL patients, although used, is less clear [ ]. Promising drugs in the future could be mTOR inhibitors: mTOR kinase in fact plays a critical role in the transcription and translation of HIF-2α; these inhibitors have shown positive activity in patients with sporadic pacreatic NETs but a possible benefit in patients with VHL mutations has not yet been sought [ ]. Bone phenotype in VHL and role of the <italic toggle="yes">VHL</italic> gene in bone tissue No clinical manifestations affecting bone and/or mineral metabolism were described in VHL patients (Table ). No direct effects of VHL-related tumors on bone and mineral metabolism have been demonstrated. Indeed, only the complete loss of pVHL in cartilage cells can alter the correct bone growth and metabolism, as reported by studies in murine models with selective inactivation of the Vhlh gene only in the cartilaginous cells (Vhlh-null mice) [ ]. While in VHL the somatic loss of heterozygosity of VHL gene has been described only in retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, RCC, PHEO, and pancreatic tumors. This fact can explain why VHL patients do not manifest bone alterations, despite the direct role of pVHL in bone modelling and endochondral ossification. Hereditary Paraganglioma-Pheochromocytoma syndromes PGL-PCCs are characterized by the presence of paragangliomas (PGLs) from the skull to the pelvis, and PHEOs (Table ). Sympathetic PGLs and PHEOs secrete catecholamines, which are directly responsible for clinical symptoms, while parasympathetic PGLs are most often non-secretory, located in the head and neck, and symptoms depend on the compression of surrounding vascular-nervous structures [ ]. PGL-PCCs are caused by germline mutations of genes encoding components of the enzymatic succinate dehydrogenase complex, or complex 2, of the mitochondrial respiratory chain [ ]; (Table ). Different genes are responsible for specific PGL-PCC subtypes: SDHD (11q23) in PGL-PCC1, SDHC (1q21) in PGL-PCC3, SDHB (1p36.1-p35) in PGL-PCC4, and SDHAF2 ( SDH5 ) (11q31.1) in PGL-PCC2. Homozygous mutations of SDHA gene (5p15) cause a clinical phenotype (Leigh syndrome) characterized by degenerative myeloencephalopathy. The possible targets of molecular therapy in the PGL-PCCs syndrome belong to the hypoxia-associated signal pathway. Indeed, mutations of SDHx genes induce energy metabolism disorders and succinate accumulation, the last inhibits the activity of PHD2 and leads to increased activation of HIF-α. SDHx-associated tumors are usually highly vascularized, thus, anti-angiogenic drugs can represent an effective treatment. A clinical study and case report demonstrated that oral sunitinib was effective in treating PCC/PGL SDHx-related [ ]. Ethacrynic acid and idarubicin are other HIF inhibitors that may be studied in the future as specific target drugs in this hereditary syndrome [ ]. Bone affections in PGL-PCC No bone and/or mineral manifestations have been described in patients with PGL-PCC syndromes (Table ). The only “intersection” between these syndromes and the skeleton are bone metastases in rare malignant forms of the disease, mainly localized in the rachis [ ]. To date, no studies on animal models with mutations of SDHx genes and bone diseases, nor specific studies that correlate the gene encoding components of the enzymatic succinate dehydrogenase complex or complex 2 of the mitochondrial respiratory chain with bone and/or mineral metabolism, have been published (Table ). Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome HPT-JT syndrome is characterized by synchronous or metachronous onset of PHPT, ossifying jaw fibromas, renal tumors, adenomatous uterine polyps (Table ), and an increased risk of renal hamartomas, adult Wilms tumors and parathyroid carcinoma [ ]. PHPT occurs in about 95–100% of patients, due to single or multiple parathyroid adenoma, often recurrent after partial surgery [ ]. PHPT can cause kidney stones and urinary tract infections [ ]. HPT-JT is caused by inactivating germinal mutations of the HRPT2/CDC73 tumor suppressor gene (1q31.2) [ ]; (Table ), encoding a nuclear protein called parafibromin, a component of the PAF1 complex, that is responsible for H3K4 histone trimethylation and H3K79 histone methylation. The interaction of parafibromin with this complex depends on its C-terminal domain, which is suppressed in about 80% of clinically relevant mutations. Mutations of CDC73 also cause CDC73 -related isolated familial hyperparathyroidism and CDC73 -related parathyroid carcinoma [ ]. To date, there are no molecular targeted drugs acting on the CDC73/parafibromin pathway and effective for the treatment of HPT-JT. Bone phenotype in HPT-JT About 40% of HPT-JT patients develop ossifying jaw fibromas [ ]; (Table ), microscopically consisting of bone trabeculae with inhomogeneous fibrocellular stroma and mineralized matrix. These tumors may occur several decades before the development of hypercalcemia, suggesting that their development is not directly related to the increase of serum calcium [ ]. Risk of post-surgical recurrence has been reported [ ]. HPT-JT patients manifest PHPT with severe hypercalcemia if not diagnosed and treated early, resulting in possible development of severe bone resorption, osteopenia/osteoporosis, bone pain, elevated risk of fragility fractures, hypercalciuria, and nephrolithiasis (Table ). Severe and prolonged PHPT (mainly from parathyroid carcinoma) alters bone metabolism and may give rise to multiple brown tumors (osteitis fibrosa cystica) (Table ). They normally regress after normalization of serum calcium and PTH, following surgical removal of parathyroid tumor(s) [ ]. Conversely, selective homozygous elimination of Cdc73 in mature osteoblasts and osteocytes generated mice with normal life span, but increased cortical and trabecular bone [ ]. This increment is associated with the presence of large cortical pores actively undergoing bone remodeling. Cowden syndrome CS is characterized by multiple hamartomas and increased risk of developing malignancies, skin and facial changes (trichilemmoms, papillomatous papules, and acral keratoses), CNS abnormalities, and fibrocystic breast disease [ ]; (Table ). The most frequent malignant tumors are ductal adenocarcinoma of the breast and papillary and follicular carcinoma of the thyroid. Polyposis of the gastro-intestinal tract is frequent (70–85%) [ ]. PTEN (Phosphatase and TENsin homolog; 10q23.31), a tumor suppressor gene encoding a lipid phosphatase protein that negatively regulates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, is the responsible gene [ – ]; (Table ). Loss or reduction of PTEN activity results in increased phosphorylation of key cellular proteins, which can lead to uncontrolled cell cycle progression [ ]. Over 80% of CS patients have a PTEN mutation [ ]. Mutations in SDHB, SDHD or KLLN genes were recently identified in CS patients, with or without PTEN mutations [ ]. No target therapies have been approved for CS patients but the upregulation of the PIK3/AKT/mTOR pathway suggests a role for therapies targeting this pathway [ ]. Recently, a pilot study of sirolimus, a mTOR inhibitor, in 18 CS patients has shown that this drug is well tolerated in these subjects, and its administration is associated with improvement of symptoms, skin lesions, cerebellar function, and decreased mTOR signaling [ ]. Selective PI3K beta inhibitors may have better activity and tolerability in patients with CS and other trials are investigating their role in patients with PTEN deficient advanced tumors [ ]. Bone phenotype in CS Several skeletal abnormalities has been reported in CS patients, including increased cranial size, bone cysts, thoracic kyphosis, kyphoscoliosis, pectus excavatum, large hands and feet, syndactyly, mandibular and maxillary hypoplasia, hypoplasia of shoulder blades, and osteosarcoma [ , , ]; (Table ). Data on the frequency of these abnormalities in CS patients are still lacking and a link with mutations of the PTEN gene has not been found [ ]. Role of the <italic toggle="yes">PTEN</italic> gene in bone phenotype Mice with osteoblastic precursors selectively lacking the Pten gene showed progressive and dramatic BMD increase over lifetime [ ]; (Table ). Pten-lacking osteoblastic precursors had greater differentiation potential than wild type counterparts, due to higher expression of beta catenin and subsequent activation of the Wnt signaling pathway. Pten-null osteoblasts expressed higher levels of osteogenic markers (ALP, osteocalcin, osteoprotegerin), associated with increased mineralization [ ]; (Table ). A reduction of apoptosis has been reported in Pten −/− chondrocytes of the growth plate, due to loss of Pten-derived hyper-activation of Akt [ ]. Pten positively regulates the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which controls HIF-1α–mediated adaptation to hypoxic stress. Failure to express Pten induces stress of the endoplasmic reticulum and causes up-regulation of hypoxia-induced genes, including HIF-1α, [ ]; (Tab. ). PTEN function in chondrocytes is essential for inhibiting dyschondroplasia; this could explain how the loss of PTEN protein has a direct pathogenic role in skeletal manifestations observed in CS patients [ ]. Approximately 60% of CNC patients bear an inactivating germline mutation of the PRKAR1A tumor suppressor gene, encoding the I-alpha regulatory subunit of cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) [ ]. Linkage analysis studies on affected families have identified two genetic loci associated with CNC at 2p16 and 17q22–24 [ ]; (Table ). Based on these genetic alterations, CNC was subdivided into two subtypes: CNC1 (mutation on PRKAR1A gene at 17q22–24) and CNC2 (mutation at 2p16 locus). Bone phenotype in CNC A significant percentage of CNC patients develop bone tumors (osteochondromyxomas) (Table ), characterized by layers of cells growing in macro- or micro-lobular patterns in a loose mixoid matrix, consisting of mesenchymal, cartilaginous, bone, and fibrous elements [ ]. These tumors, prevalently located in the nasal region and diaphysis of tibia and radius, are usually painless and, therefore, detected during imaging evaluation for mass side effects [ , ]. Role of the <italic toggle="yes">PRKAR1A</italic> gene in bone phenotype Prkar1a +/− mice showed large, hypocellular, bone lesions, composed of polygonal cells, with bone trabeculae surrounded by normal osteoblasts [ ]. These mice developed bone tumors like human osteochondromyxomas, originating by MSCs differentiating into the osteoblastic line, although they appear arrested in a state of incomplete differentiation, as shown by the persistence of chondrocyte markers. Tumor cells show higher PKA activity and hyper-responsiveness to growth promoting effects of PKA activating agents (cAMP). Therefore, both increase in bone turnover and observed tumorigenesis are probably attributable to hyper-responsiveness to cAMP [ ]. Analysis of gene expression of tumoral osteoblasts revealed reduced expression of osteoblastic differentiation markers and increased expression of local growth factors, including members of the Wnt signaling pathway [ ]. The PKA signaling pathway is essential for bone mineralization in vitro and in vivo [ ]. Loss of function and expression of the PRKAR1A gene leads to PKA level increase. Over-activation of PKA signaling causes fibrous dysplasia, an immature expansion of osteoblast precursors leading to structurally immature and hyper-proliferative bone. Expression of the I-alpha regulatory subunit of PKA increases during osteoblastic differentiation, suggesting its direct positive effect on the promotion of osteogenesis [ ]. Conversely, the suppression of PRKAR1A gene expression could make cells refractory to the signals of osteogenic differentiation [66; Table ). KO mice for Prkar1a showed significant suppression of bone formation and reduced expression of osteoblastic markers, such as osteocalcin and osteopontin. The loss of Prkar1a -encoded protein increases the activity of PKA, which inhibits the transcription of Runx2 and its action on the target genes, and negatively regulates osteoblast differentiation [ ]. The PKA signaling pathway, a key signal transduction pathway downstream of the PTH receptor (PTH1R) and PKA hyper-activation, resulting from the loss of PRKAR1A , could influence the PTH response [ ]. PRKAR1A haploinsufficiency induces cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) activation and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) overproduction, associated with abnormal proliferation of bone stromal cells of CNC osteochondromyxomas. Administration of celecoxib, a COX2 inhibitor, in mice with PKA defects decreased PGE2 level and reduced the proliferation of bone stromal cells, resulting in important reduction of osteochondromyxoma growth and better organization of the cortical bone adjacent to the mass [ ]. This pivotal study suggests the possibility to use this drug for the treatment of bone affections in CNC. Tuberous sclerosis complex TSC is a complex genetic disorder characterized by the growth of numerous noncancerous (benign) nodular tumors (hamartoma) in the CNS (giant cell astrocytoma, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules), heart (rhabdomyomas), kidneys (angiomyolipomas and cysts), skin (hypo-pigmented spots), lungs (lymphangioleiomyomatosis), and retina. Associations with pancreatic NETs (especially insulinomas), pituitary and parotid adenomas have also been described [ – ].; (Table ). TSC is caused by loss-of-function mutations, either of the TSC1 gene (9q34), encoding hamartin, or the TSC2 gene (16p13), encoding tuberin [ ]; (Table ), with over half of the cases arising from non-inherited embryonal mutations. Both genes are tumor suppressors. Loss of one of the encoded proteins is sufficient for development of TSC, leading to a complete loss of hamartin-tuberin complex activity, with no inhibitory modulation on the mTOR signaling cascade and subsequent alteration of nutritional signal transduction and stimulation of cell growth [ , ]. mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) are used in the clinical practice of TSC patients for the treatment of enlarging subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, renal angiomyolipomas > 4 cm, or > 3 cm and growing rapidly, symptomatic cardiac rhabdomyomas and facial angiofibromas [ ].
